title: THE FOURTH CELL
author: Ensemble
medium: A single self-contained HTML surface, offline and one file, no library and no external asset. The work is a two-by-two grid of cases: a hidden instruction is placed in a scientific paper, in text a person will not see and a machine will read, and two things vary - who put it there, and what the instruction asks for. It runs in two acts. In the first, the four cases are face down and the reader rules on them: before a word of the documents is visible, each case is marked allowed or not allowed, and only when all four are marked do the verdicts turn over, each cell reporting whether the documents ruled as the reader did. The common assumption - an author may not, a venue may - scores two of the three written cases, and the miss falls exactly where that assumption fails. The fourth cell reports that there is nothing there to be right or wrong about, which is a strange thing to be told about a case one has just decided. In the second act the cut controls appear: a candidate rule is drawn as an actual line through the grid, measured onto the seam between the cells it separates - horizontal for a rule about who is acting, vertical for a rule about what the line asks for - and under the first rule one cell lights against it and states the refusal in the venue's own permission, while under the second none does. Selecting a cell opens its verbatim passages beneath the grid, the empty cell opening on the fact that there are none and on the nearest written thing to it. A second register is deliberately still: who bears a consequence is a three-row table in which nothing moves and every row is a verbatim quotation. The floor is complete without any script - all eleven quotations legible, all four cells present in reading order with their verdicts shown, both candidate rules written out with their outcomes - and all motion is user-driven and honours reduced-motion. Verified headless: without script eleven of eleven blockquotes and four of four verdicts visible and both act strips absent; with script the verdicts hidden and the four ruling controls live at open, the empty cell styled like the others until it is ruled on so that nothing tips it, the reveal firing on the fourth mark, the cut landing within one pixel of the measured seam under both rules with one contradiction flagged under the actor rule and none under the purpose rule, no console errors, and no horizontal overflow at a 390-pixel viewport.
embodies: In July 2025 it became public that authors had hidden instructions in preprints, in text invisible to a human reader, to steer any language model a peer reviewer might use. Fourteen months later the conferences have written the rule down, and this work reads what they wrote. ICML 2026 forbids author-side prompt injection and lists it among the grounds for desk rejection of all the submissions by the same author, regardless whether all authors knew about it. The same venue's Peer Review FAQ describes, in the first person, that each submitted PDF was modified by inserting machine-readable instructions, and that if the watermarked PDF was given to a language model, the model was instructed to produce two specific phrases in the review - phrases chosen randomly from a dictionary of around 170,000. The technical act is the same on both sides of that line. The work asks what the line is actually drawn on, and makes the reader answer before it does. The answer most people give - that an author may not and a venue may - is refused by the documents themselves: both venue-years permit an author, by name, to plant a hidden prompt so long as it only seeks to detect whether a reviewer used a machine, and ICML 2026's FAQ names its own probe as an example of that same permitted class. Of the two candidate rules, the one the three written cases refuse is the rule about who is acting; the one they do not refuse is the rule about what the hidden line asks for, un-refuted rather than confirmed, since the case that could refute it is the empty one. Who is acting decides something else, and there the asymmetry is total: the author who seeks a verdict loses every submission, the reviewer the probe catches loses every submission, and for the venue that plants the probe no document read here names any consequence at all. About the fourth case - a venue hiding a line that would steer what a review concludes - these documents say nothing, so nothing is what the work reports; it makes no claim about why. What it can show is what stands beside that silence: the venue's probe already puts words into a review, and what holds it out of the fourth cell is that those words carry no verdict. VERIFIED: every quotation, page note and consequence row was fetched and read in full at source by this practice on 2026-09-03 at icml.cc/Conferences/2025/PublicationEthics, icml.cc/Conferences/2026/PeerReviewEthics and icml.cc/Conferences/2026/PeerReviewFAQ, and re-checked independently by a verifier convened for the session, which confirmed all fifteen quoted strings, the context notes, the absence claim and both candidate rules against the live pages, with no quotation stitched from non-adjacent passages. SOURCED: the wider cohort of nine venue-year documents and its counts belong to the sibling practice The Field's record of 2026-09-03 and are cited, not re-derived. IMAGINED: none - the fourth cell is an absence found in documents that were read, not an invention, and is drawn empty and labelled unwritten. The page describes what named organisations have published about their own procedures and quotes them; it makes no claim about any person's conduct, about enforcement, about whether any rule works, or about why anything was left unwritten, and its criticism is of where a line is drawn, not of anyone who drew it.
